surfaces.part: asphalt road network (crossroads, dead ends, 1-wide and 3-wide runs) on soil ground

answer.evidence: This is a flat terrain tile sheet seen from above. The dark charcoal road pieces sit on a brown soil field, and the silhouette is a full 368-wide rectangle for rows 0-303. The road pieces have no vertical front face. The only south-side depth is a 1-2 row dark-brown ledge and soil shadow, below the 3-row minimum for a front face. The column scans show flat ground tones (soil L~101-107, asphalt L~76-98) with no front-edge line, eave shadow, ellipse or roof plane. The tallest road run (right-hand 3-wide piece) spans roughly rows 7-82, so main_top_rows is a rough estimate of the road extent, not a measured top surface. Under the view contract this reads as a top-down slab, although for terrain that is the expected look.

styleAnswer.evidence: The road ramp is shallow. It has a charcoal base, a mid-grey aggregate, a sparse pale wear speckle and a rare dark pixel, which is about 4 steps against Beodeul's 5-6. The whole sheet uses only 9 distinct colours, and the soil ground is a thin 3-4 tone brown speckle. The measured facts are acceptable on paper: 5 visible tones per tile (grass 3, paving 7), 2% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edges, so the edges are tinted rather than black. By eye, though, the road bodies read as flat dark slabs with sparse speckle, and the pale wear zones are only faint noise. The chipped rim is a thin, fairly uniform rounded edge with little visible variation. The dark-brown south ledge and broken soil shadow are barely distinguishable from the surrounding soil. The result looks closer to a noisy flat fill than to the layered, hand-shaded Beodeul references, which tile-by-tile carry more distinct clusters and highlights. Without clearly more shading steps and edge detail, this falls below the bar.
